title: The Asteroid Heist
author: Rex Hurst
synopsis:
Subtitle: The biggest score ever pulled in the galaxy.

That’s what Jake Pool is after. He’s been across known space, pulling jobs on a thousand worlds. Mixing with dangerous thugs and murderous aliens. Always two steps ahead of the law. But it’s never enough.

Until he finds this score.

This is it. The big one!

There’s only one problem. The job is in deep space. Nowhere to run. Nowhere to hide if things go sideways. One mistake, and he’s dead.

He gathers a crack team of twelve-fingered codebreakers, cloned pirate spacers, and reptilian merc

Definition of Terms

Galactic Alliance: The most prominent ruling body in the Milky Way Galaxy, first formed as a mutual defense pact against an invading enemy bent on the enslavement of its member races

Galactic Basic: An artificial language used by the Alliance bureaucracy in all official correspondence, transactions, treaties, and legislation. It was designed to purge any individual idiosyncrasies and idioms native to one species. Thus, making it a flat sterile thing, perfect for legal work.

Galactic Alliance Calendar: Due to the vast differences between the planetary rotations of Alliance worlds and the length of their solar orbits, the Alliance lower council created a standard calendar set for bureaucratic and military business. The breakdown of time units is:

Standard Minute: 100 seconds

Standard Hour: 100 minutes

Standard Day: A 30-hour period of time.

Standard Week: 7 standard days.

Standard Month: 5 standard weeks.

Standard Year: 350 standard days, or ten standard months.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
chapters.content:
Part I – The Bid

Jake Pool darted down the marble avenues of the artificial city inside of Mylligan’s Rock. The meeting was supposed to be in an hour, but he was delayed. Someone was behind him, following his footsteps.

The shadow had been there for the last half hour, writing down every place he sat, watching every little purchase at the stalls, noting every street he navigated.

The guy was good enough to have remained undetected for a while, but he was just one sentient doing a six-man tailing job. Bound to be caught. Jake led him down some unfriendly backstreets, searching for the right spot to strike.

Jake was tall and brutish with creamy skin and flaxen hair. Most dirtbags took one look at him and ran into the opposite direction. So, whoever was following was either mighty brave or mighty stupid. Jake was gambling on the latter.

Mylligan’s Rock was well named, having been formed from the hollowed-out moon of a planet which had exploded an epoch ago. The Rock, after settling into its current orbit, was one of those places which seemed to have been around forever. Records of it dated back some fifteen thousand years.

It had gone from being an Alliance staging base, to an Orion mining town, to a military zero-gee training center, to a prison, to a failed dry dock facility, to a pirate base, and now to its current venture - the ultimate expression of the free market at play.

Several decades ago, it had been bought outright by the Orion billionaire, Asen Mylligan, who converted it into a free port. Nominally the facilities were just for use by Alliance races, but in practice Mylligan allowed entrance to anyone who wanted to buy or sell. Soon, it had become the "go to” place for any sort of illicit activity in the surrounding sectors.

Three firms of lawyers had been made rich defending Mylligan’s private property rights in the Galactic courts, and the Orion had become even richer by taking a piece of every transaction occurring on his property. And with an average of a million and a half sentients on Mylligan’s Rock at any one time, the credits racked up at an incredible rate.

Jake dipped around the corner of a back alley and waited. His shadow followed twenty seconds later. He grabbed the sentient and slammed him against the wall, hard.

It was an Orion. Similar in build to a human, but smaller, with pointed ears and seven fingers on each hand. As a professional thief, or “jobsman” as the interstellar parlance went, Jake had had plenty of dealings with the race, but rarely worked with the same one twice. When problems arose in a crew, the cause was usually an Orion.

Jake’s strength surprised his shadow. He lifted the Orion off his feet with one hand and slowly began choking the life of out him. The victim’s eyes bulged. His face turned purple.

“Ready to talk yet?” Jake snarled.

The pinned Orion nodded, his eyes showing a practiced look of confusion as if it were all a big misunderstanding. But once released, the Orion flipped out a blade and took a swipe at Jake’s nose. With ease, the jobsman knocked the weapon away and slammed the Orion’s head into the wall, face first.

SNAP.

Damn it. Broken neck. When you’re constantly jumping from one gravity to another, miscalculations about foot pounds of pressure were bound to happen. Jake had overcompensated, leaving him with a corpse rather than an intimidated informer.

Ah, well.

He went through the Orion’s pockets. Not much was there: a credit stick with twenty-five credits on it, an inject-tube filled with some sort of narcotic solution –- the Orions had so many it was difficult to keep track—, an electronic lockpick set – old style, half the frequencies were out of date— and a power shunt, which was used to short out electronic systems.

The rubbish told a pretty tale. Low-life junkie. Opportunistic thief. He snatched a datapad off the thief's wrist.

A common gadget throughout Alliance space, the wrist datapad acted as a universal communication and information storage device. By law, they had to be built to a specific industry standard so they could be used in any system in the Alliance. But that meant the weaknesses were standardized as well.

Jake used the demagnitzer on the thief’s lockpick set to remove the datapad’s face. He then produced a small cracking kit, connected it to his own personal datapad, and wired his system into the dead Orion’s unit.

DNA, retinal, and voice recognition security systems were all good protection measures, and even better when connected to temperature regulators, but they still depended on the information presented matching what was stored in the machine. If you bypassed the info storage, as Jake was doing, a sentient could reset the security system to default and then program in anything they wanted.

One, two, three. Scan. Input. Voila! The whole of the alien’s life opened like magic.

And what a loser life it was! Browser history showed mostly pornography and violent action films from the local vid flows, as well as plenty of traffic on the sports gambling sites. The Orion’s email had not been properly encrypted, but there wasn’t anything in it except spam and threats from debt collectors.

One little chat box yielded gold, however.

It was obviously meant to be deleted, originating from a burner line – a fake datapad ID meant to be used once and thrown away. The chat box held a picture of Jake from eight years ago and gave details on when he was arriving and where he was headed.

Beneath the photo were instructions ordering the dead Orion to follow Jake and let the person on the other end know if he deviated from a direct course. No reply had been sent.

Jake knew he should pack it in right then. The smart odds, the correct calculations, said the job was spoiled. If things started off wrong, rarely did they become right. And a dead body before the pitch was about as askew as it could get.

Yet, the jobsman didn’t leave. He was desperate for money. He did not simply want this job. He needed it.

It was three standard months since he last worked, and despite that job yielding a sizeable pull that should have lasted the most lavish spendthrift at least six months, Jake had all sorts of hidden expenses which had gobbled up his cut.

He knew it was a gamble to take another job so soon. Too much crime tended to draw authoritarian notice. Patterns emerged and, all of a sudden, a file you weren’t aware of was being investigated by agents of Galactic Control. But needs must as the Devil dances. He was here now. Might as well listen to the pitch.

Jake located the meet. It was a stone house, carved from marble with metal doors. The marble of Mylligan’s Rock had a natural impurity that interfered with all sound-tapping methods. Outside, it looked positively primitive. Yet Jake knew that inside, wormed through the walls like habit trails, lay all the modern electric accouterments of civilization. These structures dotted the city and were rentable by the hour.

He hid by the side of the house and sent a message along the burner line.

Get out of there! He’s around back with a pulse cannon about to blast his way in. Hurry!

The door flew open and Gurt Lynt stumbled out of the house. Lynt was another Orion and Jake’s contact on Mylligan’s Rock. A las pistol fumbled in his hands.

Lynt was an old jobsman, not really fit for duty anymore, so he earned his ill-gotten bread as a middle man. The friend of a friend. The guy who knows people who knows people. And he certainly knew enough not to pull a stupid stunt like having Jake followed.

The jobsman intercepted Lynt and kicked the gun from his trembling hands, then he knocked the Orion’s brains around his skull.

“Stop,” Lynt cried. “I’m sorry. It wasn’t my idea.”

Jake hefted his fist. “That so?”

“It was Cullidan. He insisted. And I figured what’s the harm? Put the guy at ease.”

“Put him at ease?”

Jake filtered through his memory. The name Cullidan didn’t pop up. By itself that didn’t mean much. Across the galaxy there were probably millions of competent jobsmen Jake hadn’t heard of. Yet, a new name should always be met with caution.

“Lead the way,” he ordered and pushed Lynt into the building.

It was a four-room structure. Two exits. No windows. The inside was carpeted on all surfaces to keep the natural clamminess of the stone at bay. Seated on a plush divan was a member of the last race Jake would have ever expected to be involved on a job. An Eridani.

Eridani culture was a rigid caste society with the warriors on top, supported by the noble houses. Whenever the Eridani were about aliens, they were supposed to be representing their race to the “inferior peoples” of the galaxy. Any slight to one them was a slap at the entire culture. Every game became a test to display their superiority. Even a casual round of checkers could become a tension-filled violent exercise when the Eridani were involved.

The few Eridani Jake had met were career military. Upright figures in peak physical condition. Not a hair out of place. Not a button unpolished. In the ten years Jake had been pulling jobs, he had never met a crooked Eridani. It just didn’t happen.

Until now.

There was something sick and seedy about this specimen. His race’s coloration tended towards a deep yellow. Yet Cullidan’s was darker, like old urine, and a sour smell lingered on his collar.

Cullidan wore no military or house insignia, which was unusual for an Eridani. The clothes he had on were slovenly, uncleaned. A distinctive pot belly flopped about his midsection and his arms were ropey, the flesh sagged off them. If he had ever exercised, the effects were long gone. He sure as hell wasn’t casting his race in a positive light.

“Come on in,” Cullidan said. “Pull up some air. We’re just waiting on the other guy.”

“The one following me?”

“Not that idiot. He’s just a stooge.”

“Good, because he’s dead.”

Cullidan’s eyes jumped. He tried to cover it by adjusting the breather mask on his face, but the sentient was clearly rattled. The Eridani were natural methane breathers. Oxygen was poison to them. There were rooms for rent in the city with a methane atmosphere, but he had chosen otherwise.

Lynt eagerly ran over and helped him with the mask. That was another odd thing. Traditionally, Orions and Eridani hated each other. The reason stretched far back in time to some ancient battle, but these two seemed to have gotten over their racial prejudices.

Jake settled in a chair and relaxed, as much someone like him could relax. He took in the pair who were laughing together over some private joke. Even the Eridani’s name was twisted, he realized. It should have been Culli-iden, but somewhere along the line it had been corrupted.

“So, what’re your back pulls?” he asked Cullidan. “Who do you know? Besides Lynt there and I don’t consider him much of a character reference after today.” The elder Orion pouted, but said nothing.

“Let’s just say, I’m dangling a hoop.” A translated Eridani phrase meaning he was a newbie. “One plan. One big idea. Then I will happily saunter away on the cosmic trails.”

An amateur. Probably with a grudge to settle. Perfect. A perfect storm of shit that is.

Jake rose.

“What are you standing tall for?” Cullidan asked.

The entrance buzzer rattled a dying tune. The house’s electrics obviously needed some work. Lynt went to the door and let in Aleister Song, a human. That was good. Jake had worked plenty of jobs with Song. Even if he could sometimes be a bit silly, Jake trusted the man’s ability absolutely. Had anyone else been at the door, Jake would have walked. Now, he had someone to confer with.

“Not to alarm you all,” Song said, “but I was followed on the way here. Don’t worry. I killed the guy.”

This sparked a hubbub of explanations, recriminations, arguments, and bad feelings all around. Song thought pretty much as Jake did and seemed determined to walk out, until Lynt pleaded with them.

“You’re here. Just listen to what he’s got to say. It’s different, I tell you. Something never done.”

“That doesn’t mean it’s any good,” countered Jake. “Usually there’s a reason something hasn’t been done.”

Cullidan tried to put on a friendly smile, but he was obviously furious. He obviously hated being disagreed with.

“I’m told that you’re one of the best. That’s what I need here. Consider what we talk about a rough draft, then we can edit the plan with your knowledgeable input.”

“It’s a three-man job then?” asked Song.

“We’re gonna include Lynt along with the rest of us. But consider yourself captains. I figure the whole job is gonna need about twenty in total.”

Jake and Song exchanged alarmed looks. That was as big of a red flag as they could imagine. Was it now strike three, or ball four? Either way, it made Jake balk. He began listing Cullidan’s mistakes, raising a finger sharply after each point.

“One, you’ve proved you don’t trust us by putting tails on us. Know the kind of people who do that? Untrustworthy ones. Guys who think everyone’s trying to rip them off, because that’s exactly what they plan to do to everyone else.

“Two, you’re an amateur with, I’m guessing here, a personal motive for hitting your target. That means there’s an additional purpose beyond profit. A further link between you and the crime. Which is one extra potential clue you’re giving up to the whoever looks into it.

“Three, too many involved. It’s difficult getting a good crew at the best times. With twenty, the slots will have to be filled by second cousins, green newbies, or idiot wanna-bes. You get more than five on a plan, one of them will screw it up somehow. Maybe they’ll tell the little lady and she runs at the mouth. Or one of them brags about his big job to impress a stripper and she tells the hod –”

“The what?” Cullidan asked.

“Hod. Police and whatnot,” answered Lynt.

“Or one gets picked up for something stupid and rats on us. So, we go under because some jerk can’t stop committing petty crimes,” finished Jake.

Cullidan rubbed his chin. Anger, arrogance, consideration, and confusion took turns dancing across his face. He obviously wasn’t used to being corrected, certainly not as much as Jake had just done, but he was smart enough to realize the jobsman knew his profession.

“Let’s talk about the target and see what you think.”

They adjourned into the next room. Jake saw the place was double laden with security devices. All sorts of gadgets had been wired in to prevent eavesdropping through electronic or psychic means, that was in addition to the house’s natural immunities. No wonder the electrics were having a hard time. It was total overkill. The only way someone could listen in here would be to literally put their ear to the keyhole.

Holograms flew from Cullidan’s datapad, filling the air in the middle of the room, displaying plans and schematics of an asteroid base. It was all very detailed, hot-off-the-presses information. Jake recognized the basic configuration as an Asteroid Mining Corporation outfit.

“This is Maze Base One,” Cullidan began, “located in the Maze of Orion belt. Twenty thousand miners are housed here. The biggest camp in AMC’s territories. Three stone towns make up the central area, each on a different asteroid. One is for personal quarters and recreation. One is for mineral storage, vehicle repair, and parking. The third handles administrative duties, system housing, guidance, and security details.”

Cullidan went on and on about the base and its parent company. The name pretty much said it all. The corporation, through bribes and efficiency, had cornered the market on asteroid mining, forcing their rivals to strip-mine planets for valuables. While on the surface a planet might seem like a richer field to plunder, a lot of problems popped up on larger spheres that just didn’t happen with asteroids.

For one, the constant entering and leaving an atmosphere put considerable wear and tear on vehicles and equipment, adding to costs. Even orbital shots, where the material was thrown into low orbit and scooped up by shuttles, weren’t as cost effective as never having to leave zero-gee.

Additionally, whenever a corporation started tearing up a planet that supported life, or could possibly support life in a million years, all sorts of hippie-dippie groups came pouring out of the patchouli-soaked woodwork to protest. Often, they snuck in little clumps of morons to sabotage operations and cause general mayhem. No one worried about asteroids.

Cullidan went on about the internalization of materials and company script, expenses, recreation, and communication between the base and its parent substations, plus those com channels required by Galactic Naval safety guidelines and other bureaucratic legal decrees. Tons of paperwork, media, and informational data was beamed back and forth between the base and government agencies.

Jake kept waiting for the Eridani to get to the point. He figured the score was a load of valuable ore, or some magical alien artifact, or an uncovered supercomputer from a forgotten war, but Cullidan just blathered on about communication methods. Then it dawned on the jobsman what the object of the mission was.

“You’re out of your skull,” he declared.

“Am I?”

Song looked around. “What am I missing?”

“He’s suggesting that we rip off the whole of the digital payroll for Maze Base One. Every six standard months they rotate a quarter of their miners out for mandatory gravity rehab and transmit their money with them.”

Of course, Jake knew it wasn’t just the payroll being transmitted. Banking could be a long and difficult process in the void of space. To save on the astronomical costs of using the Stargate coms systems, many credit transactions from the sale of ore were transferred from station to station and stored until a scheduled Stargate transmission was ready. They were possibly talking millions here.

Song whistled, a human trait Jake found irritating for reasons he couldn’t identify.

“What an idea,” he said. “Couldn’t really work though.”

“Really?” the Eridani laughed.

Then he filled them in on the rest of the plan.

Afterwards, Jake sat isolated in a corner of the marble house, going over the details, categorizing them into mental folders then rearranging them, looking for flaws and faults. All the refreshments he had accepted lay uneaten, undrunk, and unsmoked on a low table before him.

Right then, the biggest flaw he found was still in the man rather than the play. Apart from his slovenly attire, two other things really stuck out about Cullidan.

Eridani were unforgiving about failure. Their race’s Buddon code required them to commit acts of self-mutilation over any screw up. Penance scars, they called them. Cullidan had none. Not a nick. Not a scratch. No one goes through life without screwing up once. Not unless they blame everyone else for their mistakes.

Secondly, an Eridani’s hair, its color and style, represented a person’s position in society, or his mindset or mission. In the repressed caste world, hair was symbolic of worth and purpose.

Cullidan was bald. His race didn’t naturally go bald, that much Jake knew, so he must’ve had it shaved off. Pretty much a massive ‘screw you’ to the whole of his society.

When Jake later mentioned these points to Song, the human had just shrugged.

“So? We’re thieves. Jobsmen. None of us is beholden to any set of laws or customs.”

“But we don’t look like criminals,” Jake put in. “You wouldn’t pull a job with a sentient who had ‘thief for life’ tattooed on his head. That’s pretty much what we got in there for an Eridani.”

Jake and Song left Cullidan to his empty rental and dancing holograms, retreating to a nearby greasy spoon to deliberate. Lynt slunk around them like a puppy dog looking for a pat. He received none.

After the waitress served up their bladder burgers – made from the internal organs of mutated zebras – and warm Horrokroshcu milk – all the rage in this sector – the trio got down to their deliberations.

Lynt was all about the money.

“It’s a stellar score. One of the biggest ever. But, as you saw, his plan is screwy, with his wanting to get a battalion of jobsmen for this. Typical Eridani. Always thinking in military terms. That’s why I insisted on you two. You need to iron everything out and make it feasible.”

Song was in awe of the idea.

“Money’s good, but think of the audacity, the daring it would take. That’d be worth doing on its own. It’s never been done. It’d be like pulling the first moving train robbery.”

The grandeur of Achilles shone in his eyes. His head wasn’t on the job, but the story afterwards. The books, the vids, the endless chatter over the flows about the caper. Glory, glory everlasting. Jake slapped the human’s mind planet-side.

“You can knock that crap out of your head. The only way this gets big is if they know who done it, otherwise you only have half a story. I’m not getting identified so you can become a paragraph in the galactic crime encyclopedia next to eternal shit-heels like Jackisarious Phentari.”

Jake, for all his misgivings, thought mostly about how much he could use that money, about how many problems could be alleviated with that much loot in his grasp at one time.

And even though the red flags kept waving, in the end he knocked them aside for the very real reason that the job was doable.

But only if he took command. Only if all the jobsmen were picked by his own hand. And only if every nut and bolt was checked and double checked personally by him.

“I don’t like this Alliance Naval Tracking Station orbiting on the edge there,” Lynt was saying, displaying a sector map on his datapad. “It’s an equal distance to the Stargate, and if it picks up an emergency signal from the base, it can override the gate’s systems and whistle for a cruiser to blow us all to our respective hells.”

“I know those bases,” Jake stated. “They’re entirely automated to cut down on costs. With a few signal interceptors placed about it, we can block all transmissions for a decent chunk of time.”

Song and Lynt bit into their bladder burgers. Jake left his untouched. Both tried to hide their smirks, but Jake’s saw.

“Something funny?”

“Does that mean you’re in?” asked Song.

“Guess so.”

Later that night, Cullidan poured out a concoction that smelled like it was dredged from the bleach pits of Hell. The liquid was ambrosia to the Eridani senses, deadly poison to any other race. The Human and Orion picked up booze suitable for their races and saluted the enterprise to come. Jake used an empty glass.

The mission was all on the jobsman’s shoulders now. One night to rest, then off to collect the men and the tools.
