Part II – The Prep

The Tich

Due to regulations, all interstellar corporations must deal in standard Alliance credit currency. Institutions given licenses to bank and trade in that credit were heavily regulated by the Alliance and chosen only after the most intimate scrutiny was completed, or a sizeable enough bribe was presented. These safeguards were in place to prevent an economic collapse of literal galactic proportions. As such, demand for sanctioned banks far outstripped supply.

When dealing with an asteroid mining operation, there is almost no chance that such a financial institution will be located anywhere nearby, but accounts still have to be maintained. Income, outtakes, payroll, regulations. The books must be balanced on a regular basis.

The routine tour of duty on an asteroid mine was six standard months, then the workers were shipped out for a two-month vacation – without pay, of course – to allow their bodies to readjust to a regular gravitational pull. Otherwise, their muscles and bones would begin to irreversibly atrophy.

When a worker shipped out, all of their information was transmitted to a nearby Alliance approved banking establishment. In the case of Maze Base One, time was booked on the local stargate com systems to transfer it to a bank on the planet Transit.

The plan in a nutshell was to invade the coms section of Maze Base One and repurpose the outgoing banking transmissions into several accounts of the jobsmen’s choosing – albeit still on the planet Transit. They couldn’t alter that part.

Unfortunately, this was not something that could be hacked from afar, the base systems had fail safes on top of fail safes. All such banking transmissions carried various subspace Alliance security identifiers to prevent forgery. The crew needed to get in there and physically change the transmission destinations.

That is where Jake had initially seen failure.

“That payroll transmission must be an automatic command locked into the coms unit,” he had said. “Meaning you need override codes to alter where it goes, then reroute thousands of individual accounts. That’ll take too long. And if you don’t have the codes or if they change them at the last minute, we have to torture some guy for the new ones which means it takes longer. Then security comes down and a firefight happens.”

Cullidan had smirked at that and sipped more booze.

“You’re forgetting that all these AMC units are plug-and-play. They don’t waste money on redundancies. The coms unit is not where the accounting is done. All of the digital ledgers are sent via hardline into the coms unit which sends them out blind to the Stargate.”

“That makes it sound more difficult. Another set of pass codes. Another place we need to occupy.”

“Except that it’s standard policy for AMC to use Cwi-X78 converters to connect secure hardlines between units. Everything flows through it and I know for a fact no one has bothered to change the passcode on the converter since installation. We can intercept the material and alter destination codes right before it’s all collated into one transmission burst. Course, we’re gonna have to shop around to find the best device…”

Nom would know, Jake had thought.

Which was what brought him to a store near the residential sector of the city. The place was thick with little flying buzzing things that lit up and made weird noises. These weren’t spy cams or anything sophisticated, just RC devices people bought for their children.

Jake had never played with toys, so he completely missed the point of them. Not that he was even remotely interested in the pastimes of others. The place was irrelevant. The owner was not. “Nom, where are you?”

No answer. The store itself was almost entirely automated. Everything was arranged around a self-checkout stand stationed next to the door. Jake could feel hidden security cams rolling over his skin. The floor practically bristled with electric panels which would stun any shoplifters.

“Nom!”

The back wall shuddered open, revealing a tinkerer’s paradise. Tools, bits of electronics, crystal lattices, wires, fiber optics, ion burners, and shortwave converters were scattered everywhere. Six half-constructed devices of indeterminate purpose stood prominently on a similar number of workbenches. Cutters, welders, scanners, and polymer injectors hung from the ceiling above each one.

A wide purple face with a red beard as thick as a beehive slid into view. Nom grinned through rotten teeth. He was a Goola-Goola, a sentient from Gnoosie in the Heinock star cluster. The Goola-Goolas were technologically advanced, but had the organizing capacity of a pile of kittens. Their home planet was divided into thousands of loose city-states with no unified currency or government.

Goola-Goolas were welcome to travel, work, and even live in Alliance space. Special visas had been legislated to allow them in, but the race had no representation in the Alliance government. The Goola-Goolas didn’t seem upset by this.

“Well, Mr. Pool,” Nom said, wiping something sticky from his hands. “What bits of fun are we interested in today?”

The Goola-Goola listened carefully as Jake laid out the details of the mission, smiling with delight as the massiveness of the job manifested. Like Song, Nom was more interested in the achievement than the score. He began digging through old crates shoved in the rear of the workshop, pulling out various pieces of electronic gear.

“Most of the hardware will be standard for a break-n-crake. Thermal dampeners, code crackers, power shunts, and so on. For the Cwi-X78 converter, since you have the codes, you’re going to want to utilize a device with speed. If it takes too long, an alarm might get raised. That’s a minimum of thirty thousand alterations in five seconds. Not easy.”

Nom was what they called a Tich, an Orion term adapted into modern jobman’s slang. It meant a supplier of illegal technology useful for committing crime. As time marched on, the Goola-Goola race seemed to be cornering the market on this job.

Nom pulled a metal box from the table with a few wires and clamps dangling from it.

“Pretty straightforward. Hook your datapad in and enter the new material. It should just have enough oomph to alter the signals before someone notices the holdup.”

Jake handled the box and ripped off the top, making sure it was not full of loose wires. He took in the circuitry, most of it barely above the molecular level. Very sophisticated. Very powerful.

“Very nice,” he said and handed it back.

“One snag. It has to be attached directly to the converter in three places. Part of its power comes from leeching off the Cwi-X78’s own backup battery. You can’t tap into the line. Meaning someone needs to physically get into the grill works and attach it.”

“No problem,” Jake said. “I got a sentient in mind.”

“That isn’t the real problem though,” Nom said, then went quiet, waiting for a response.

Jake didn’t bite. He didn’t believe in dramatic pauses and simply stared at the little purple man until Nom continued.

“It’s to do with that Alliance tracking station near the asteroid belt. Just ‘cause it’s automated doesn’t mean it's stupid. I reckon twenty-seven signal interceptors will be needed to blanket the station. The interceptors will also have to be disguised as regular asteroid debris. The problem is in the placement. The signal system will detect and instantly register any unusual activity. All the interceptors have to appear to drift into place through natural momentum. The only way to do that is to hand guide them.”

“Hand guide them?” Jake asked.

“You’ll need someone in a heavily shielded ejection bubble to drift just out of signal range and roll them in place with an injection scoop calibrated with enough torque. That way all twenty-seven will orbit the station naturally. A hell of a job.”

Indeed, it was. And it just might be the straw that broke this camel's back. It was not a job Jake would volunteer for. If anything went wrong, that man would be the first sacrificed.

“You got a body for that?” asked Nom.

“No.”

“Good, then I volunteer.”

That was a surprise. “You? Have you ever pulled a job before?”

“I won't be part of the regular heist. Just drop me off, let me work, and pick me up.”

Jake was up against the wall here. Nom was a great Tich, no denying it, but that didn’t mean he’d be any good on the job.

He’d seen it before. Amateurs hitching along who suddenly think they can act any which way because they’re about to commit a crime. Most end up doing something stupid, getting caught, and spitting up everything to the hod.

In this case however, the needs of the job outweighed the potential problems. Frankly, there was no one else but Nom to stick into the slot. Jake reluctantly agreed.

“How much?”

“Just like everyone else. A pluth up the open division.” That was a Goola-Goola idiom, roughly translating to “a piece of the action”.

They shook on it. Jake’s most sacred vow.

The Slip

There were five stone towns, underground cities, founded when Mylligan landed. Each had been divided up by what they offered the market. Here in Yoncuar - which translates to Hightown from the Orion tongue - one could buy all sorts of materials that did not require a physical presence. Access, intelligence, various other deniable services. It was also the perfect place to meet with someone about a future job.

The city had been built into an artificial cavern, hollowed out from a massive marble deposit. The cavern roof was sixty feet up to prevent all those nasty mental illnesses every species seemed to develop when enclosed in small places for too long. The illusion of natural light was obtained from massive photospherent balls hanging overhead that let off all of the radiation of a yellow dwarf star. It almost felt like real sunlight.

With no natural atmosphere, each of the stone towns maintained its own biosystem. Nuclear powered bullet trains raced down tunnels between cities. The only signs of civilization marking the surface were docking bubbles and signal relays to aid in landings.

Jake watched a ship bearing Lynt and Song being lifted towards a docking bubble. It was destined for Transit, where the data currency transmissions would be beamed. Their mission was to establish dummy accounts at the banks on Transit for short term use.

The term “dummy account” here was a bit of a misnomer, because they had to be as real as possible. Song and Lynt had spent the last two weeks putting together their false identities. Despite ever tightening controls and refined security measures, it was impossible to stop identity fraud with a population in the hundreds of trillions spread across several galaxies.

The best way to do this was with DNA masking, where a virologic containment web was implanted under the skin which gave all modern ID devices a false DNA reading. It was painful to endure and took about a week to fully spread throughout the body’s dermis. The web lasted four months before the body destroyed what it saw as a biological invasion. Song and Lynt would establish accounts under their false DNA patterns.

After they were gone, Jake descended into the bowels of Yoncuar’s sewage and energy producing subsectors to meet with another invaluable asset to the team. At least, this team.

This job was bringing out all sorts of usual types. Most of the time Jake would not have had any use for this sentient or his kind, but as he had long suspected,

Under the right circumstances, anyone can be useful.

He bypassed a security door with skilled ease and plugged his nose against the stench of the city’s underbelly. Before him was an old machine used to regulate the sewage system. Thousands of pipes connected to enclosed vats where the effluence of a hundred races mixed together. It was sturdy but slowly slipping past its prime. Even with daily checks on the seals, a foul smell managed to wriggle out.

Once a vat was full, it compressed, sucking up all of the oxygen, methane, and other useful gases, which were then shunted off to other facilities for recycling. The rest was then spat up onto the surface of the rock.

Once a month, cleaning crews would float out and chisel away the mountain of feces piled up around the ejection hatches, depositing the stuff on another part of the hollowed-out moon.

Around the machine’s base was a mass of slick gray stone. At least, it appeared so at first glance. But as Jake watched, he saw the mass shift and move and heard light rhythmic tapping.

“Swip Tum-Tum,” Jake yelled.

The gray mass writhed. The tapping increased in volume and violence. Bubbles blew on the surface.

“Swip Tum-Tum. Get out here or I call security. None of you are supposed to be in this section and you know it.”

That did it. All of the gray pulled together into a horizontal mound on the side of the sewage machine. From its top, a ball spat out. The thing rocked back and forth for a moment, then rolled up the stairs to Jake. The rest of the gray settled back down.

Jake took out a small harmonized device and stuck it into the ball. The gadget allowed the two races to communicate.

This was a Mazian, a creature which had no natural bone structure, sense organs – other than its dermis – or even organ sacks. It was as it appeared, a giant blob. Mazians did have a central ganglion mass which seemed to act as a brain, but it was nothing you could point to on the outside.

Mazians normally communicated by tapping on the ground, the race being particularly attuned to sonic vibrations. Dull loud thumping, like the one pulsating from the sewage machinery, being the most pleasant to them. The harmonizer translated the creature’s tapping into Galactic Basic.

“Got a job which you might fit into,” Jake said. “I mean that literally. We need you to squeeze into a tight area and handle some equipment.”

“I think that’s something I can manage,” the synthetic voice replied.

One of the drawbacks of the harmonizer was that it gave no hint of mood. Some said the Mazian’s had the ultimate poker face, but Jake knew it was only a matter of checking the creature’s texture to see their emotional state. Right now, Swip Tum-Tum’s surface was folding back on itself, over and over, indicating excitement.

Mazians were unique in being the only sentient race to never have developed a technology, not even Stone Age devices. When they were first discovered, the race hadn’t even bothered to develop the wheel. Why should they? They could roll themselves anywhere.

“You’ll be able to handle work on a Cwi-X78 converter? You’ll be rewiring part of the hardline and inserting some delicate instruments.”

“Sure. As long as I get a little practice, I can slip in anywhere and do and what needs done.”

There was a reason why Jake had never used this species on a job before. A Mazian was a self-contained animal. It easily digested leftover organic matter in whatever state of decay. It had no natural predator on its home planet and sported a tough dermis which could withstand temperatures between -25- and 190-degrees Fahrenheit without discomfort.

As it stood, there was no reason for the Mazian to do anything but tool about and absorb food scraps. That’s what troubled Jake, the race had no real needs, no vices to exploit, no families to threaten.

So why was Swip Tum-Tum going along?

“Fun!” it said. “Besides, you're a good guy. I’d like to help you out. You don’t even have to pay me.”

Jake balked at that. It went against every one of his jobman’s instincts. This would be a life-or-death situation. Why else would you do it if you weren’t getting paid? The transaction of wealth, in one form or another, is what made one a professional. A sentient who came along just for the adventure was sure to cause problems.

“Don’t worry,” the Mazian kept saying. “We’re pals, aren’t we? I’ll do it gratis.”

Pals? Jake didn’t have pals. He had colleagues. The people he knew were just that, people he knew. A means to an end. Ones who could help him pull off the next job, that’s all.

Jake didn't have a personality that engendered friendship, or warmth, or love. What it did generate was trust. Trust in his skill, his planning, and him holding up his end of a deal.

No one ever wanted to have a beer with Jake, but when he ran a job, everyone got their percentage. In the long run that meant way more than how much people liked to socialize with him.

So, who knew where this Mazian was coming from? Maybe he was deranged. The psychology of the race wasn’t really understood, if it could ever be by non-blobs.

Jake put his foot down. Swip Tum-Tum needed to understand the running of things right then.

“You’ll take your percentage. You’ll act professional. No goofing off. No exploring. You’ll do your job to the letter and nothing more, or else I can’t guarantee I won’t be forced to kill you. Understand?”

“Absolutely,” was the flat synthesized reply. The blob’s skin had stopped folding.

The Doze

The flier, or doze in criminal argot, would've been called the getaway driver back in the olden days. It was a ship’s pilot who could, after a job, blast the crew into another solar system before anyone knew what was going on.

Decent piloting skills were an obvious must, but a good doze also knew how to avoid the staggering amount of detection sweeps which could be employed. He had to know what an enemy was likely to use and have a countermeasure in his bag. That meant constant updating and continuous research. For this heist, the doze slot was crucial. There would be no hiding on the asteroid base. They either got away or they were all dead.

Jake took a bullet train across the gutted moon to Bloncauer, or “the Boardwalk” as some called it. It was the gambling district where the greatest casinos in the galaxy glittered.

Bright and shiny objects sparkled in every direction. Dazzling people, dazzling meals, dazzling events filled every crevice. But Jake noted that not two blocks away from each of these embedded jewels of excess were several layers of flop houses, pawn shops, blood banks, and even a few organ harvesters, that circled the casinos like giant bathtub stains.

Jake did not like gathering everyone he needed on one sphere, lest some overzealous investigator start piecing things together, but the free port of Mylligan’s Rock was almost made for jobsmen. He knew that Galactic Control most certainly had agents in place, noting down who came and left, but there was little the agency could do to prevent crime.

He had heard a rumor that the entire place was in fact a Galactic Control operation. That the tens of thousands of people working here were employed by that interstellar police force and every centimeter was bugged. They said, one day the signal would come down and, SNAP, the entire moon would be arrested.

Jake didn’t pay any mind to this. Considering how much illegal activity he saw on a daily basis, he figured Galactic Control would have to shut down all other operations and spend decades in the courts prosecuting the events of just one solar cycle.

Jake entered The House of Numbers, once a massive system-sharing scam, it had turned legit and gone into the numbers racket on the other end. All forms of games of chance lay about. It was all pleasure here, as long as you kept gambling.

He walked to the far end rooms. Sports from the other side of the galaxy were beamed in for the patron’s delight and misfortune.

“Goddamn son of a bitch. Get the ball!”

When the Human race’s fertility rates fell into triple negatives, various Alliance powers had worked together to create a viable alternative to the species. Lest one of the most ardent supporters of the Alliance, and its ongoing war, go extinct.

The result was the Gen-Human. Faster, stronger, smarter, and better looking than the original, Gen-Humans were able to mate with their sire species and eventually would strengthen humans as a whole.

These were not clones. Force-grown to maturity in vats, pre-programmed with a skill suite, and sent to work, each Gen-Human was a unique individual, culled from sperm and ovum. It had to be done this way, otherwise all sorts of genetic redundancies would begin popping up in future generations of humans.

“Get the fucking jammer up there! Parley it to the hangman. Parley! Parley! You fucking morons. Can’t move, even in zero-g.”

Gen-Humans were contracted to corporations for their first twenty years, then became free agents, able to forge their own destiny, able to work for whomever and even change their name. Which led to Jake’s contact coming up with…

“Johnny Rocket.”

“Jake Pool? Holy shit! Sit down. Have a drink.”

Unfortunately, the tech boys had yet to find a way to genetically engineer good taste. Jake pushed away the drink offered by a hovering drone. He wanted to get Johnny’s full attention, but the game on the center screen had the Gen-Human completely enthralled.

“Tell me Jake, what are you doing here?... What the? Garbage goal, man. It was out of the crease! Are they recruiting blind men to ref?” He waved away Jake’s non-existent rebuttal. “I know it's all done by A.I., but damn. Maybe they got grease on their lenses.”

The game Johnny was glued to was Cyball. Its goal, like ninety percent of sports, was for one team to get an object into an opponent’s zone. Two teams were entombed in a giant cylinder in space and needed to negotiate a ball through a rotating playfield filled with hazards.

Jake never paid attention to Cyball or any other sport. The idea of gambling money on its outcome seemed wasteful. Still, he respected the game’s popularity and never spoke against it. He even pretended to have a favorite team, the Alleged Sentients out of Louistin, in case anyone asked.

Jake waited.

“Go, go, go, go, go, GO! … Ah, shit!”

And waited.

“Jesus Christ. How many bounces is this thing gonna do? There ... Get it ... Idiots!”

Until finally,

“Game over, man. My life is a black hole of pain.”

Johnny Rocket buried his head under his arms and wept drunken tears. The display at the table registered that the Gen-Human had just lost five thousand credits on the game. Guess you couldn’t genetically engineer common sense either.

But whatever his faults, Johnny Rocket was a first-class doze, which is what kept Jake at the casino. The jobsman cleared his throat.

“Oh yeah,” the Gen-Human pulled himself up from self-pity. “Did you want to talk to me?”

Jake went into the job, while Johnny downed another drink. The Gen-Human’s eyes narrowed during certain parts, but was nodding along by the end. He slammed the glass down.

“Count me in. Just a couple of odds and ends need to be handled.”

“Like what?”

The Gen-Human’s voice changed. It was all business now.

“I’d need to look over whatever schematics you have. I need to double check, but I can probably lock into the landing bay. Holding it however, if there’s a problem, might be tricky. I’d be much happier if we bought a couple of defensive missiles – nothing out of the ordinary for AMC vessels – just to ward away any heroes. Let me show you the types I mean.”

On his datapad, he pulled up various units for sale on Mylligan’s Rock. The numbers were outrageous, but what price safety?

The pair shook on the deal.

“When do we go?”

“About two months.”

The Thumps

Now that the technical positions were filled, all that was needed were some extra thumps. That is, pure muscle. Jake usually waited until the end to recruit these because idiots who could shoot and give a beating were a-couple-a-credit in a galaxy that had been at war for the last twenty years. The other spots were specialists, prima donnas. Now, he just needed to fill in the chorus.

Technically he, Song, and Cullidan, filled these positions, but Jake wanted a little extra something to tip the balance, and he had just the two thugs in mind.

Jake jumped a further bullet train to Glocaeur – or Lowtown – the leftover area which was used for housing support staff, security workers, technicians, and various other wage slaves who maintained Mylligan’s Rock.

At the city, Jake hopped a transport tube over to the slummiest area of the slum city and stopped at a rock shack missing its front door. All the houses on the street were a one room affair, sharing a communal toilet at the end of the lane.

A massive viewscreen dominated the inside wall. It was tuned to a puerile game show called, “Urinated on From Above”. The action was pretty self-explanatory, and it certainly amused the two gargantuan lizard-men lying on the floor eating fast food from a plastic bucket.

The Urd Brothers were Ram Pythons from the planet Pythos. Their actual names were Jai and Peh, but no one used them. They were so damn close in appearance most sentients couldn’t tell one from the other, but as they were always hired together, no one ever had to learn.

Even Jake’s precision brain had to admit they were practically identical. The only obvious differences being the color of their eyes. One was brown and the other slightly darker brown. But he didn’t like to buck trends and simply yelled, “Hey Urds,” along with everyone else.

“Knock knock,” Jake said.

“Who’s that? You ready for a beating, Freddy?”

One of the pair loomed in the doorframe holding a massive quarterstaff tipped with barbed metal on either end. When the lizard spied Jake, his green lips broke out in a grin, showing several layers of carnivorous teeth.

“Jake Pool,” one Urd said. “Are you here to give us more money? You never stop by any other time.”

“That’s why we like to see you,” chimed in the other.

Jake was offered some deep fried splukoliish from the bucket, but waved it away. He had no idea what splukoliish was, nor was he in a hurry to find out.

Mostly the Urds worked as part-time bouncers for the rowdier bars, but Jake had found them useful in a few jobs. They took orders and did not ask questions. Perfect thumps.

Rams hadn’t progressed beyond the Iron Age when the Alliance had come roaring down from the skies onto the planet Pythos. Suddenly, their culture went from worshiping their sun to blasting between stars, from hammering metal by hand to donning synthetic polyscene armor rolled off an automated assembly line. This jump in technology, far beyond the ken of most of the race, is what gave the Ram Python their reputation for stupidity.

The Urd Brothers were a little smarter than others of their kind. Having been raised on an Alliance-run world, they were at least literate and could do basic sums – pretty much all that was required from the Alliance education camps. That had not stopped them from going bad in the end, but at least they could read the charge on the docket when being hauled before a judge unlike most others of their race.

Jake kept to the basics of what he needed from the Urds, not mentioning any potential problems or using words of more than two syllables.

They agreed, because of course they agreed. They never had to exert themselves much on any jobs run by Jake in the past, so why would they have to now? He gave the brothers an address.

“We’ll start training for the job next week. Make sure you’re there.”

The Cip

For the final part, Jake needed to take a trip down to see Roddy the Cip, a human who had never seen Earth. Roddy had spent most of his life jumping from one illicit rock to another. A cip handled all sorts of incidentals for a job. IDs, costumes, even weaponry on occasion. Since the plan required the team to board an AMC base, they needed to look the part.

“That’s no problem,” smirked the Cip. “Best thing about AMC is they run everything on the cheap. One-size-fits-all uniforms. Economy IDs. Nothing special about the fabrics. But I think you’re in extra special luck today.”

On the outside, the Cip’s shop looked like another stone bungalow, but hidden beneath it was a mechanized vertical warehouse, consisting of a series of boxes and platforms hooked around conveyor belts, synchronized to a keypad. A number was tapped in. A box rose from the depths. No records were kept. Everything in stock was lodged in the Cip’s head.

What ascended was a plastic box with AMC markings across it. The Cip popped the crate’s top, revealing about forty AMC special security uniforms, complete with boots, helmets, and gloves.

“These are the genuine article. Salvaged off of some ship debris over at the battle on Stilt. The Galactic Navy conscripted every ship to fend off the enemy’s assault. None made it. For a while, it was a field day for scavengers.”

“We’re gonna need IDs to go with it.”

“Easily done.”

Jake gave the number and races of those involved, excluding Lynt and the Mazian. They quickly settled on a price and the uniforms were shipped.

Jake was satisfied. Everything was handled. No more planning. No more recruiting.

Now, they just had to do the job.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
chapters.content:
Part III – The Go

Jake peered through the viewscreen at the massive rocks floating by. The Maze of Orion was an asteroid belt discovered by the Orions – in case you were confused about that – hundreds of years in the past.

What made this belt stand out was its sheer size. Most asteroid belts were the remnants of failed planets, ones that had not congealed properly under gravity's gentle crushing. In this case, an estimated six to seven failed planets made up the Maze of Orion. Multiple theories existed as to why this had happened. None had been proven.

The target, Maze Base One, lay on the other side of the belt. Jake and crew were using the Maze’s density to hide themselves from both the mining facility and the automated Alliance signal base.

Nom was in the docking port, making last minute checks before being tossed into space. Right now, the Goola-Goola was fiddling with his main ejection bubble.

Ejection bubbles were meant to be last minute survival gear in deep space. A back-up’s back-up. They were what you used if your survival pod failed. It came with a modicum of pressurized air and nothing else.

They were cheap, but not very effective. An estimated ninety percent of people who used them died. Either from asphyxiation, dehydration, starvation, or debris popping the bubble. It wasn’t that they were badly made, it was just that if you were ever in a position to need one, help probably wasn’t close by.

Nom had modified his extensively, adding oxygen scrubbers to recycle the air, emergency powder rations, plenty of water, plus some propellant canisters to help shoot the bubble in the direction he wanted. The purple alien had little spherical signal interceptors strapped all over his body. Those, along with an injection scoop covering one hand and various other pieces of homemade survival gear made him look like a walking junkyard monster.

The Goola-Goola gave the thumbs up. “Let’s show ‘em,” he said over the squawker with a wink and was flushed out into the frigid nothingness of the void.

We are here to go. The words flew up through Jake’s unconsciousness. It was from an old Earth poet, which Jake’s former – let’s say handler – was fond of. Jake didn’t really understand it, but every time he saw a sentient leap into the oblivion of space, the words returned.

It would take several hours for Nom to reach his position and start rolling the signal jammers into place. This was the waiting time, the calm before the storm, when anticipation nibbled at a man’s nerves and everyone’s bowels loosened just a bit.

The toilets quickly became overused, especially after both of the Urds took a turn. Johnny Rocket, like a good doze, had thought of this and put backup flushers at the ready.

Jake did not partake in them, much to Song’s seeming amusement. He spent all his time examining every aspect of the plan, as he had a thousand times previously. The jobsman didn’t have an uneasy feeling or anything like that, but had learned from experience that thorough preparation was the best way toward success. And that meant constant review.

Try as he might, Jake could not come up with a flaw. That was not to say there weren’t any. No plan survives contact with the enemy. But wherever the fault might lie, it was beyond Jake’s ability to control.

They had spent the last two weeks going over and over each step. Cullidan, as the backer, had balked at some of the expenses, but only a little. He would be repaid tenfold after the pull was split.

Jake had even rented out holo-suites on Mylligan’s Rock and ran mock drills through them, using the known configurations of AMC modular base units.

That was where Cullidan tipped his hand. The base had been in operation for so long, a full half decade past its estimated abandonment date, that various patches and make-shift workaround units had been created by the staff. Cullidan knew them all. The crew adjusted accordingly, but it only compounded Jake’s suspicions that the whole job was personal for this wreck of an Eridani.

He’s a weak link and yet we can’t get rid of him. At least not until the job’s done.

Everyone was in their AMC special security uniforms. They had rigged together a security transponder on the Asteroid Mining Corporations reserved frequency and installed it in Johnny Rocket’s ship. All the travel passage codes were supplied by Cullidan.

The ship was disguised as a personnel crawler and repainted in AMC colors. The back half of the vessel was simply sheet metal covering the backup ion generators, which gave the ship double the power and thus quintuple the boost when activated. They would be kept hidden unless pursuit was at hand.

One hour. Two hours. Three.

The men shifted, snorted, scratched noses. Everyone looked apprehensive except the Mazian blob. He was quiet, apart from an occasional bulge rising to spit out a pocket of air from its innards. There was no small talk, no pep talk. Just flatulation and silence. Each sentient engaged in some sort of mental trick to pass the time. These were experienced jobsmen. They all knew about the interminable wait, wait, wait before the go.

“Pinpoint laser signal from Nom,” Johnny Rocket yelled. Smart move. There was no way to intercept that transmission except on a direct line. “He’s in position. Starting the roll.”

Which meant the waiting period began over again. They weren’t going to hang around the entire time Nom was floating in the black, but he needed to get at least fifteen interceptors into position for them to begin to work.

Dead silence. Burp, sniff, cough.

One more hour. Two further hours. Three agonizing hours.

More shuffling. The jobsmen twitched in their seats, counted spots on the ceiling, adjusted and readjusted the straps on their armor, measured their weapon’s charge for the fifth time. All while they clamped down on their urges to do something god-damn-it, something other than just sit here!

“Laser signal,” laughed Johnny Rocket. “It’s go time.”

He kicked on the ship’s ion drives and headed towards the mission. When the jolt of that initial thrust hit them, all the jobsmen breathed easier. Finally, they thought.

Maze Base One was constructed from three clamped together asteroids. Massive titanium pylons, embedded deep into the rock, kept it all in place, while flexi-steel tubes transported people and materials from rock to rock.

Everything in an AMC mining operation was standardized. A paint-by-numbers affair. Even the creation of an initial base’s stone town was fit tab A into slot B. A suitably large asteroid was chosen, then hollowed out to specifications. The predetermined number of needed units were plugged in, screwed together, then sealed up. Instant city. Need an expansion? No problem. Plug in a few more units or move to the next asteroid and repeat the process.

The Maze of Orion was one of the best profit centers for the corporation, not so much because of the material, but due to its position.

As races branched out into the depths of space, they usually found that whatever mineral was rare on their planet could be found in abundance elsewhere. Thus, as the profiteer said,

“It all comes down to distance.”

What a mining area yanked from the rocks was just as important as how close the base was to colonized planets. Planetary manufacturing tended to stick to whatever that terrain yielded. However, shipyards and other space bound construction plants found it easier to haul in ore via stargates and the standard shipping routes than dredge it up from a planet. The closer the mines, the less it cost.

Johnny Rocket’s ship spun around the asteroid belt, affecting a travel signature parallel to a vessel having just come out of the stargate. They skirted into the base’s short-range signal radius, an area where the corporation could blow you away and legally claim self-defense.

“Broadcast coming in,” reported Johnny. “Let’s see if these codes were worth the price of admission.”

“They’re all good,” Cullidan sneered.

The Urd brothers grumbled. Jake cooled them with a look. The Eridani certainly hadn’t wasted his time worrying about being liked or respected. Jake didn’t agonize much about the former either, but he devoted a lot of running time to being respected.

Cullidan didn’t care what anyone thought about him – and not in a good way. When not training, the Eridani had either been drunk beyond senselessness, headed in that direction, or spitting venom at everyone around.

“Okay,” Johnny Rocket said, “docking permission granted. Pod two as we wanted.”

“Gear up,” Jake commanded. “Helmets on. Visors tinted. Give them as little to see as possible.”

“Bay doors open,” reported Johnny. “Hold on for gravity transmission.”

Everyone grabbed a strap. Johnny’s ship had artificial gravity, as did most modern space vessels, but it needed to be switched off when the ship entered a secondary field, otherwise gravity would suddenly double, causing damage to man and machine alike.

They passed safely through the base’s bluish-hued gravity screen, which automatically kicked in after the docking doors released, and settled down on a raised glowing dais. Everything pressurized. The jobsmen fell into ranks. The ship's hatch began opening.

“You’re up, Song,” said Jake.

Drops of sweat formed a perimeter around Aleister Song’s brow, threatening to run down his face. He had been picked for this part, not due to his acting ability, but because he was the only one who could reasonably squeeze into the stolen AMC special security officer’s uniform.

Lynt might have fit better, but he was on Transit. If they were caught but the money was successfully diverted, he would still be able to retrieve the loot and sit on it for when the others could collect. At least, that was the theory.

The jobsmen all fell in behind him, except for Johnny Rocket who wasn’t leaving the ship. Song presented his fraudulent credentials to the Docking Chief and Security Officer, who tapped their toes waiting on an explanation behind this intrusion. The Chief scanned the falsified ID code and projected it against Song’s genetic helix.

One second. Two Seconds. How long was this supposed to take? Three seconds. Did that security guy just look at him funny? Four seconds. The Docking Chief frowned. He knows! He knows it’s all fake! Five seconds. Song gripped his gun handle. Jesus Christ! Gotta put a hole in this fucker’s face.

The Chief gave Song back his creds.

“Sorry about that. Energy pack is going on this scanner and it went into power-saver mode. Slows everything down.”

“No problem,” Song answered with false nonchalance.

“So, what’s going on here?” asked the Security Officer. “There’s been no deaths. No thefts. We’re ahead of schedule on ore extraction. Why are the big boys paying us a visit?”

Song took a deep breath. He’d rehearsed this bit of babble and the possible replies for hours. He’d gone over it so much that the words had lost all meaning. He might as well be jabbering a host of nonsense cadences.

“More corporate espionage. Caught wind of a doppler strain on the last few transmissions. Looks like someone’s trying to crack our codes and interfere with the running system.”

“But that wouldn’t be happening on our end,” the Security Officer objected. “There has to be at least a dozen signaling stations between here and Transit, not to mention the stargate systems themselves.”

Song shook his head sympathetically.

“Orders are to check every place down the line, including here. Local security is to stand down on this matter.” The Security Officer was about to object, when Song put his hand up. “I understand. I wouldn’t like it if I was on the other end, but this is the way it has to be. You could complain, but Corporate will just repeat what I’ve told you.”

“All a waste of time,” the Chief muttered.

“I know. I agree, but let’s just get it over with and then tell them that.”

The Security Officer well understood AMC’s policy of “orders are orders” and, since his lunch was growing cold, waved the Special Security Detail through without much more thought. These things happened periodically in a large company. Best not to let it get to you.

Smugness claimed Song as they marched on up to the Communication Unit. Job damn well done. Jake could not have handled it any better, was incapable of doing it, Song mused.

He respected Jake, had followed him in on this job without hesitation, and trusted his tactical ability, but Jake Pool wasn’t all he appeared to be on the outside.

It had taken a while for Song to catch on. While the sentient looked human, something else was going on. They had worked six jobs together and eventually he picked up on all sorts of oddities about Jake’s behavior, which had then led to a startling conclusion.

But right in the middle of a job wasn’t the time to confront him about it. He’d have to wait till it was all wrapped up on the planet Transit.

The moment they were out of earshot of the landing bay, Jake reasserted command. Not that he needed to give any orders. They had all rehearsed it so much, muscle memory alone could have carried them through.

The Communications Unit was a 1300 square foot section, mostly taken up with machinery, and was designed for a maximum crew of five. Like every other section on the base, it was modular and could be hermetically sealed off and detached if needed.

The jobsmen hit it like a thunderbolt. Through his past jobs with Jake, Song knew just how to handle the situation. It was a three-point assault.

1. Strike fast and quickly. Always use the element of surprise.

Which was just what happened. Only four crew were on duty when the jobsmen stormed the section. The Urd brothers grabbed the startled people and herded them together in the center of the unit, not giving the crew any time to set off any alarms or scream their idiot heads off.

One woman tried to get up and run, but Jake planted a hard fist into her solar plexus and down she went, mouth flapping like a gasping fish. Each crew member had a weapon barrel stuck in their face. Jake issued a harsh command:

“Anyone tries anything, they die.”

2. Lock things up quickly and keep it cool.

The Urd brothers took guard outside the section doors to make sure no one entered. Luckily, the jobsmen didn't need to coerce any of the crew for a code or to fake an ‘all clear’ signal. They just needed to be restrained so they wouldn’t be underfoot.

“Now, we’re going to tie you all up,” Jake said, his voice eerily level. Song had seen him calm down some pretty hysterical people with this tone. “As long as you don’t resist, try to get away, or call for help then you will be fine. If you do otherwise, the only thing you’ll accomplish is your own death.”

Each crew member had their mouths gagged, a bag placed over their head, and hands bound behind their backs with sealant foam – a spray gel that hardened within seconds to a density matching cement.

3. Keep discussion to a minimum and don’t get distracted.

Everyone had a job and this was not the time to improvise. The Urd Brothers were to keep any stray crew out of the section, which they would do with as much force as required. Cullidan needed to prep the arrays to send the signal as normal. Swip Tum-Tum, who until now had been hidden in their equipment boxes, needed to squeeze between the machinery and slip their little sabotage drive onto the Cwi-X78 converter. Song handled the security feeds, running maintenance checks and fouling them up for the next half hour. Jake supervised everyone and made sure the prisoners did nothing stupid.

So far, everything was fine. Everyone was doing their job. It was smooth. Damn smooth. Too smooth. At this point they had practically gotten away with it. A spending frenzy went on in Song’s imagination. I’m sure nothing will –

Song yanked back the thought mid-sentence. Cockiness only provoked the Gods of Karma into messing with a body. Had he just jinxed himself?

It wasn’t easy for Karen Hobbs, coms technician third grade for Maze Base One, to hold in her bladder, but she didn’t dare ask the large man holding a rifle to her head for a potty pass.

Who were these lunatics? What kind of psychotic attacked one the biggest corporations on their own turf? The answer to that caused her to leak a little.

Terrorists. Rebels. ARM. Mercenary saboteurs from a rival corporation. Savage killers, willing to blow themselves and any innocents around to Hell’s icy depths in order to send some pathetic political message that everyone would ignore.

She was almost relieved when they put a bag over her head. If she couldn’t see them, she couldn’t identify them. That meant they were less likely to kill her.

Didn’t it?

Karen was laid out on the floor, presumably next to her co-workers. Soon, it seemed the invaders relaxed and started talking. She would’ve shut her ears if the power was gifted her, but the coms tech was forced to lie there and listen.

“Song, double check that the security overrides have taken. Sometimes the system twitches and needs to be reinserted,” said a voice speaking Galactic Basic with an Eridani twang.

Was that ...?

“No names,” a gruff voice barked. “Get the blob into position.”

“Disabling the security links now,” the Eridani voice said again. “Refilling it with maintenance spam…. There, security will be blissfully ignorant unless they’re physically told.”

It was! Cullidan!

From her perspective, it sounded like the invaders were tearing panels away from the walls. What the hell were they up to? But who could say with her former boss at the helm. His presence did not make her breathe easier. He was an incompetent, big talking, micro-manager whose solution to each problem was screaming at everyone.

She only hoped he hadn’t noticed her, or that he wasn’t fully aware of the details of his dismissal. Because it was Karen who got him fired.

The drinking on duty had been bad enough, but when he moved onto hard drugs … well, let’s just say she had an intense case of schadenfreude turning him in. All it took was a “random” drug test and out he went. No goodbyes and no sorrow from any of his underlings.

What was he up to with this group of deranged killers? Or whatever they were. Nothing good, nothing healthy, she was sure.

Oh boy. Oh boy.

Squeeze. Push. Tuck. Roll.

Swip Tum-Tum was having a hell of a time. It imagined itself on the battlefront among other great Mazian warriors, storming the skies, striking down the enemy threat. True, this was only a criminal enterprise, but it was action nonetheless.

Up, over, push, squeeeeeeze.

Swip Tum-Tum rippled his skin along the electronic guts of the transmission apparatus and dragged itself forward. The area it needed to find was only ten yards from where the Mazian had been stuffed into the works. However, the space was packed with machinery with not a centimeter wasted.

Forward. Forward Down. Sliiiide. Puuuuull. Up. Up. Up.

It was a complicated maneuver. Normally, the Mazian could flatten out a lot thinner, but the rig it carried added too much girth and it was forced to take a roundabout route to the Cwi-X78 converter.

Tuck. Push. Push. Slither up. Slide down.

Swip Tum-Tum didn’t mind the strain. It was doing a vital part of the mission. One that only he could accomplish.

Onto the beaches. Into the tunnels. One Mazian stood against them all. With skill and guile, the enemies’ defenses fell before the magnificent blob. He let out a Mazian piping tune used on occasions of great joy. The race sang by pressing air through folds in its skin, so every symphony sounded like a collection of armpit farts, but Swip Tum-Tum found it inspiring.

Bend. Corner. Corner. Kitty-corner.

If only the place wasn’t so damn dirty. The crew obviously had never gone into the inner guts of the apparatus to clean up after installation. The amount of filth and gunk was just incredible. It would take a week to scrub the particles from the Mazian’s skin. And then….

Uh oh. Stuck.

From Jake’s position, things were nominal. The prisoners were under control, everyone was doing their job, and security was blissfully ignorant. It looked good, but this was no time to relax. At this point, the job all hung on the Mazian blob – an amateur. And it was getting near transmission time.

“Two minutes,” Cullidan reported.

The Eridani was puffing through smokes like it was the last hour of his life. Jake didn’t mind that. The stress of the job, the increased rush of adrenaline, or alien equivalent, had strange effects on the body. If it kept the Eridani calm, let him smoke. Jake just made sure that Cullidan took all of his butts with him so he couldn’t be later identified by DNA left on the filters.

“One minute forty-five seconds,” Cullidan said with a hint of irritation in his voice.

“Skip the countdown,” Jake ordered. “Just let us know when it's done.”

As he had previously noted, everyone else had done their part. It was all down to the Mazian.

Great. Just great, thought Swip Tum-Tum. First job and I’m too fat to squeeze through.

Swip Tum-Tum’s dreams of being the great Mazian jobsman were dripping down the drain.

Pull. Pull. Puuuuul. Make it through, no matter how much it hurt. Edges bit into the Mazian. It could feel its flesh tear, its liquids leak. Shockwaves of pain rolled through its dermis.

Pull. Pull. Pull.

It wasn’t going to lay down. Not Swip Tum-Tum. Did Thump-Thump Ting quit during the Battle of Aciacon when it ran out of ammunition? No! Did Swoosh Tup-Tip roll over and die when left exposed in the arctic wastes of Hoolidoon? No! And did Pop Snap-Pup, the greatest living Mazian military commander, give up when its ship was floating dead in space after destroying five enemy vessels.

HELL NO!

Crack. The Mazian was...almost there… almost there ... arrgh … pain … nearly … pain … nearly … pain.

SNAP.

Relief. Relief. A casing the Mazian was stuck on bent back and broke off the metal struts holding the machinery in place. The equipment banged about, sending sparks flying, and made one hell of a racket. Still, Swip Tum-Tum was free. That was all that mattered.

As the Mazian rounded a corner, there lay its goal. The near mythical Cwi-X78 converter. The object of the quest. The blob surrounded it and pulled out the rig Nom had put together.

Now… what was it supposed to do next?

Culidan crushed out another smoke. It was his twenty-seventh since they’d taken over the unit. The Eridani wasn’t nervous. He was angry, legitimately boiling over pissed off and he had no idea why. It had started with the clockwork precision in which the group had taken and held the area.

The job was running smoothly. Too gods-damned smoothly. Jake had done his work too well. There would be no muss, no fuss. They’d all be orbiting another star before the corporation’s hounds even knew something was wrong. And once the fraud was found, the authorities still wouldn’t know who had hit the base.

That was the problem, he realized. Culidan wanted all these stinking desk jockeys to know who had ripped them off, who had torn apart their pathetic security.

He should never have let Jake take control. Mercenaries were plentiful in the Alliance. That is who he should have hired, a bunch of killers. Because that’s what he really wanted to do. Blow this place up and shoot all the smug fucks populating it.

Maze Base One was filled with scum, always talking behind his back and smirking about his family. His entire life they had been doing it, the faceless masses just out of range, a heartbeat from earshot. He heard them hidden around corners, behind window blinds, under manhole covers, even outside portholes in the vacuum of space.

Cullidan wasn’t quite sure of their identities, but this damn gaggle of conspirators had ruined his life. First, they had denied him acceptance to the most basic military academies in Eridani territory, meaning that he would be ineligible even for his own family's honor guard. The lowest of the low in military terms, yet a position which would have allowed him a smidge of respect.

After that, his family conspired to throw him out, forcing him into degradation of having to join the private sector. He knew for some races success in business meant joining the ranks of society’s cream, but for an Eridani it meant being cast as a second-class citizen.

There were further pits one could tumble towards in his culture, but Cullidan had side-stepped them by leaving Eridani controlled space and entering the Alliance workforce. He thrived for a time after joining the Asteroid Mining Corporation, taking management and technical courses and rising to the rank of Shift Supervisor of the Coms Unit at Maze Base One.

Of course, he hadn’t really escaped his tormentors. The evil bastards were just setting him up for a great fall. He was fired publicly, stripped of his pension, and black-balled in the corporate world. They didn’t even have the decency to kill him. They wanted to slowly drag out his painful existence until he committed suicide.

That was when Cullidan decided to stop playing their game and found Lynt. But now he realized what they had put together here was not good enough. These vermin needed to pay. Not just in money, but blood and flesh.

The Eridani played with a plasma grenade hooked on his belt.

Roll, roll, roll.

The stout purple man floated in the vacuum and aimed the device snapped onto his wrist. It was just like bowling the feiran when he was little – a pastime of many young Goola-Goolas, involving ricocheting a stainless-steel ball off of twelve sticks.

It required just as much knowledge of angles as it did skill. Nom had been pretty good back in his teens. Not professional good, but decent enough to beat the kids in his neighborhood. Back then though, the penalties for failure were only a few jeers from the other children. Here, a screw up meant, at best, twenty years in an Alliance penitentiary. At worst, death in the endless void.

Yet, he was not afraid. The weightlessness, the soundlessness, the odd bobbing of his body, calmed him. He placed a spherical signal interceptor into the injection scoop and made the calculations.

Eight more degrees along the y -axis, make sure it overlaps with the previous interceptor on the Py-rotations. There would always be some movement in the spheres, which is why it was important for their signal dampening arcs to intercept.

Yep, that was it. Go.

The sphere shot out of the scoop, rolling in an arc. His wrist datapad checked the thing’s flight. With no inertia in space, he modified the interceptor’s movements with little CO2 canisters. Otherwise, they would keep on traveling and eventually go out of range.

The pad lit up green. It was in position. He sent the stop signal and the canisters went off, slowing the ball down little by little until it ceased moving. Number twenty was in place.

In the distance, the tracking station remained dormant. Nom thrusted gently forward, looking to the base’s sensors like just another rock gliding through the universe.

The ejection bubble tugged along behind him like a giant placenta. A host of tubes connected the pair. Air hoses, and the backup air hose, and backup’s backup. Nom was nothing if not methodical.

This is great!

He had spent too long preparing others to go off on their various illegal operations. Year after year, tough sentients, the backbone of the Alliance, who forged the path to civilization – or not – with blood, steel, and plasma had come to him for help. And while at least half of them never came back, Nom couldn’t help but admire their courage.

Secretly, he’d always longed to go on one of those expeditions. To loot treasures of a forgotten world, or burn out a secret enemy nest, or be a part of a high-stakes heist. Things were winding down for him. Soon he would be past his prime, unable to keep up with technological trends, and thrown into the junkyards of tech-past like most elderly Goola-Goolas.

Before this opportunity, he had made do with old films of action and daring. He prized his complete collection of Spiff Blasthandy tri-vids. Now, he would have a real story and real memories of ripping off some corporate fat-ass.

Hmmm.

Was it his imagination or did the external lights around the station’s docking ports suddenly illuminate?

Time was ticking. Swip Tum-Tum could tell it was close to zero hour. It ran through the procedure. Connect the device, siphon the battery with dual 56t clamps, recypher the crystal matrix, and then boot up an alternate processor rigger. It did all that and …

Nothing.

The Mazian was pretty sure there was supposed to be a noise when the battery siphon powered up the processor. A beep of some sort. But there wasn’t.

Damn it.

It should have paid more attention during training, but Swip Tum-Tum had slacked off that last week, figuring it didn’t need more.

They’re gonna kill me.

It had no choice but to try again. Connect the device, siphon the battery….

Beep!

There was the needed noise. Oh, happy days! Swip Tum-Tum could breathe again. The device heated up. The alternate processor rig started to hum.

That was it. Everything was done. The only thing left was to slither back and collect the money.

“Transmission data received,” Cullidan reported. “Collating now. Just a few seconds.”

Everyone but Jake visibly tensed. This was the last moment. The last chance for some Cosmic Trickster to dip its sticky fingers in and gum up the works. Maybe a technical fault in the transmission apparatus would occur. Maybe Nom’s gadgets weren’t compatible with AMC’s systems due to an unforeseen software update. Maybe someone in the group had sold out the rest.

“Collated. Loading transmission package,” Cullidan’s eyes scanned the screen, while the others hung onto the Eridani’s words. “Loading still … Finished … Transmission away!”

Had they brought champagne, the cork would have popped right then. All the tension built up over the last two months leaked away.

They had done it!

The Mazian squeezed out of the ducts and rolled around, slapping everyone’s hand with a meaty pseudopod. Even the Urd brothers came in and shared the joy.

It was a well-earned moment and Jake let it go on, but soon he snapped everyone back to focus. After all, this was just the tipping point. In a real sense, the job was only half done and any jobsmen worth the name knew not to relax just yet. No celebrating until the money is in your hand.

“All right,” Jake ordered. “Start the cleanup and let’s get out of here.”

It was then he noticed Cullidan had snuck off.

With the small facilities available on the base, it was always mealtime for someone. A small kitchen, a small cafeteria, meant everyone had to be allotted their regulation meals within a limited window. Three squares for each crew member were served within a twenty-hour cycle. The room was continuously full. Cullidan hung in the doorway, watching the workers eat.

There they were. All the scum. All the villains who had stabbed him in the back, stolen his future, and shat on his name. A great desire seized him. He wanted to crack skulls, bite through knuckles, dismember knees, burn genitals, and taste the blood of every bastard chowing down as if nothing had happened, as if they had never conspired against him.

They needed to be ripped to pieces, their bodies beaten to blood pudding, then he would move on their families and continue to kill even unto the third and fourth generations of these vermin, the ones who had done him wrong. He itched to take one of his weapons and just open up on that crowd.

And as he thought it, the plasma grenade was in his hand. And before he could consciously connect what was going to happen, the sphere was flying into the center of the room. And before he could thoroughly enjoy the mayhem, fifteen sentients were burnt to death when superheated plasma blew through them, while a further twenty-five went down with severe burns and missing limbs.

Not a bad start.

Cullidan unslung his laser carbine and started finishing off the survivors.

When the explosions and screams began, Jake knew he was going to have to blast his way off the station. He was ready for that, even if it wasn’t the ideal exit plan. In fact, it was the worst-case scenario, apart from shipping out in a body bag. A lot of people were going to die. A lot of heat was destined to descend on their heads. Jake shot an emergency signal to Johnny Rocket through his datapad then hefted his pulse rifle.

Clean-up was supposed to take up to an hour, with the team splashing caustic substances on every inch of the section to wipe out any trace of DNA. But there wasn’t time for that now, so Jake was forced to order,

“Burn it.”

White phosphorus grenades were utilized, engulfing the entire coms unit in flame. Everything that could burn, did – including the unlucky technicians. They cried pitifully and writhed about as the substance ate through their bodies, reducing it to hot ash and greasy smoke.

Jake would have preferred it otherwise, but he had to be cautious. The Urd brothers didn’t seem to care. Song was disturbed, but professional enough to bottle it away.

Swip Tum-Tum… well the blob’s body wasn’t shaking or twitching at all, which could mean one of a dozen emotional states. Not that Jake was too concerned about the Mazian’s comfort. There was no time to pack the blob away, so it was tossed a laser and told to shoot straight.

“Can he even hit anything?” asked Song. The blob wasn’t manifesting any eyes.

“He can hit whatever he wants as long as it’s not one of us. Let’s go!”

Jake took the lead. The others fell naturally in behind him, weapons at the ready. There was no bullshit now, no bluffing through. Any obstacle was to be taken down with maximum force.

The station was on full alert, which meant chaos reigned among the lower ranks. Alarms blared. Automatic “keep calm” announcements blandly told people to follow their emergency lockdown plans, but most of it was lost under howls and yelling.

Fistfights broke out. The overhead lights flickered for a few seconds. A screeching half-naked woman ran past. Workers scampered down the halls, arms filled with stolen stationary. They saw the group’s uniforms, and backed away. Only security was allowed firearms, so even if these crewmen wanted to fight, they couldn’t.

A head popped out of a latrine.

“Is it true? Is it true?” the worker asked. “Is there a Flying Guillotine on board?”

“Yes sir,” Jake responded. “Better get ba—”

The door slammed. A warbling cry of fear leaked through.

It was like that all the way through the station. Workers caterwauled. They cried. They hid in weird places with half of their bodies awkwardly hanging out. Some seemed obsessed with stealing. Others got drunk and threw bottles at people rushing by. The crew pretty much did everything but follow its emergency protocols. Either the base had fallen way behind on its disaster training, or else no one had paid attention while it was being conducted. Jake had no complaints. The chaos worked in his favor.

“Halt!”

Two security guards with standard issue AMC laser carbines blocked their paths. One yelled out in a commanding voice.

“You are to lay down your arms and –”

The sentence was never finished. The Urd brothers immediately opened up. While the security boy’s laser carbines were good, they were squirt guns next to the lizards’ pulse rifles. Souvenirs from the Urd brother’s stint in the Galactic Marines, the pulse rifle fired accelerated plasma through a magnetic bottle powered by a miniature fusion reactor which unleashed an explosive force. Useless at long range. Deadly in small corridors and cramped space stations, as the two security men found out. Their bodies smeared the walls. A few solid bits and pieces remained behind, but most of their corpses had become scattered jelly.

Another member of security was spotted trying to break up a fight. Song put a well-placed hole in the man’s head. They came across a further security man drunk under a desk. One of the Urds was about to kill him, but Jake stopped the lizard. The man was too insensible to be a threat.

One guard was encountered coming out of a toilet area. She was velcroing her pants up when she saw them. A dumbfounded look sprouted over her face. Jake put her down with one quick blast to the neck. Otherwise, there were no other immediate obstacles.

The real trouble waited for them in the docking bay.

One more dead. One more enemy fell to Cullidan’s wrath. Every race under the umbrella of the Galactic Alliance had fallen at his feet. A rainbow assortment of blood swirled across the floor. Gods, he was alive.

“ALIVE!”

This was the only true way for an Eridani to live. Cutting down enemies. Driving the weaker species underfoot. He channeled his ancestors, the heroes who had forged his house, and the Gods from Beyond who had bequeathed all of known space for the Eridani race to dominate.

“The steel of my sword cuts with a swiftness of a heart that is never dulled,” he roared, quoting an old Eridani maxim.

On the floor, a human tried to pull his guts back in. Five shots exploded his head like an overripe fruit. He spotted an Orion cowering under the table, using a plastic tray to ward Cullidan away. He shot the creature in the groin, then, after suitable laughter, again in the heart. A poor Goola-Goola ran away, trying to defy fate. Two blasts to the ankles ended the retreat. Another in the skull finished his life.

“I do not bleed, because I refuse to!”

Heavy footfalls came down the corridor. Military commands were issued in Galactic Basic. Another plasma grenade tossed down the hall ended that noise. Cullidan peeked out. It was security boys this time, splattered across the deck. Bits of the dead men had embedded in the ceiling. Gore dripped down from above.

One wasn’t quite dead, though much of his life was pouring from the stumps which used to be his legs. Cullidan loomed over his prey, feeling quite the predator, and cut the man’s throat. The power, ohhhhh the power, just thrilled him.

He caught sight of another man darting through a T-junction. The Eridani pounced after him, pondering whether he should shoot the man outright or play with his guts for a bit. He turned the corner.

Twelve carbine barrels stared him in the face. Cullidan, the “mighty warrior”, immediately dropped his weapon and stuck up his hands.

“I want to see a lawyer,” he whined.

They answered by pulling their triggers.

The docking bay was a disaster area. The emergency lockdown alert had come down just as Johnny Rocket received the alarm code from Jake. In a lockdown situation, security wanted everything contained and unable to move so they could easily isolate and eliminate trouble. That meant all spacecraft would be hit with magnetic clamps to keep them immobile. The only way to avoid the clamps was to be aloft when they snapped.

And Johnny had done just that. Unfortunately, taking off without guidance permission and hanging around in a sealed docking bay made it painfully obvious exactly who was the object of the security alert.

When the jobsmen entered the bay, all other shuttles had been crippled and most of the docking crew were dead. Security had tried to shoot the rogue ship down, but had gotten the worst of the battle and were barricaded in the control booth. Twisted metal and burnt corpses hung about like Christmas ornaments.

“We’re here,” Jake signaled Johnny Rocket via his datapad. “Scoop us up.”

“No can do,” the doze replied. “The bay doors are shut. You have to take the control booth and open them. The booth’s blast shields are down and the lasers can’t penetrate it, so I can’t help you get in, but I’ll try to keep any other security boys off your back.”

Jake conferred with the others.

“Can we squeeze the Mazian in via the ducts?” asked Song.

“No. Once those blast shields are shut, the whole box is self-contained with an independent air supply,” Jake replied. “That’s in case the bay is opened into the vacuum of space. We can’t bluff our way in either, since that’s obviously our ship killing everyone.”

“Then we just blast it open,” yelled an Urd.

A typical Ram Python response and probably the quickest way to crack the mystery of the locked box. Jake agreed they had to do it.

But where to find enough explosives? An idea, a desperate one, hit Jake. He did some quick mathematics and confirmed it was possible.

“You’re going to hate this,” he warned Song, then signaled to the doze. “Detach and drop one of your missiles.”

“What the hell are you doing?” yelled Song.

“We’re gonna use the warhead to blast into the control booth.”

“Are you crazy? It’ll take out the whole booth and the hangar door will still be closed.”

“Not if we tuck the warhead in the far corner of the bay. The door of the control booth will be destroyed, but most of it will remain intact.”

“And our ship will be crippled as well.”

“We’ll have Johnny Rocket stick his ship in the opposite corner, as far as he can cram it. It’ll take damage, but I’ve calculated it should survive. We can’t have him fire one, because the thrust will push the blast too far into the structure to be of use to us.”

“You’ve calculated that, huh? The yield and radius of the missile’s warhead,” sneered Song, but then caught himself. Of course, Jake Pool had. The sentient had the capability. “Let’s do it,” he said.

The Urd brothers jumped into action with no complaints, mostly because they really didn’t understand the argument. If Swip Tum-Tum had a problem, he kept it quiet. No one would have listened anyhow.

The crew started the process of removing the warhead from the delivery system without blowing themselves up. It wasn’t that tricky. The missiles were built with secure safeguards to prevent accidental detonation. The Urds burned through the joints with acidizers and high-gauge blowtorches.

Metal fell away at a steady rate, but it was taking too long. Johnny had to repel a security team attempting to invade the bay. Jake wished Nom was with them. The tinkering Goola-Goola probably would’ve had the whole thing done in half the time.

Once they placed the bomb, the jobsmen would need to retreat back into the base proper to avoid the blast radius.

“How do we know this isn’t going to blow a hole into outer space?” Song asked.

“Those bay doors are double thick, and the rest of the base is built into solid rock. It should be all right.”

“Should be?”

“I’m doing the best I can,” Jake snapped uncharacteristically. “I’ve heard nothing but complaints and no ideas come out of your mouth. This is the only plan we have. You can either shut up and trust me or go kill yourself.”

Shocked, Song stopped talking and doubled his efforts. Jake never acted like that. It had to mean they were closer to death than ever before.

Finally, the warhead slid off. An Urd brother caught it before the explosive device hit the ground and quickly stashed the payload in the corner where Jake pointed. The jobsmen reached in and placed a detonator next to the missile’s explosive element. He sent the activation code to Johnny Rocket then rounded up the crew.

Now, they had to punch their way back. Taking in the tensile strength of the metal structures, Jake estimated they needed to be at least three hundred yards away if they were to survive the blast.

As the group retreated, Jake considered reinforcing his “don’t hesitate to shoot” policy, but there was no need. Everyone was on edge and popped off at any movement.

‘What’s that?” Song yelled.

All the jobsmen shot. Some air was singed. A few leaves were singed off a plant.

“Stay frosty,” Jake said.

One hundred yards.

Move on. Move on.

The area was now empty. It looked as if the crew had decided to follow their emergency training after all. All the hatches were hermetically sealed. Except for the blaring alarm, there was no noise. No shadows flickered. No movement at all. Yet, Jake knew security was there, hiding somewhere, waiting to ambush.

Two hundred yards.

Move on. Move on.

Laser fire erupted from a junction. One of the Urd brothers was hit, but not down. The jobsmen returned fire, taking what cover was available. Back and forth the shots went, with none of them connecting. Neither side seemed able to hit the other. Suddenly, Jake caught some movement on the other end of the corridor.

They’re trying to surround us. Mow us down in a crossfire.

He checked his datapad gauge. Three hundred yards in. Right on the line. It was a dicey call, but they couldn’t afford to get boxed by a pincer movement. He signaled to Johnny Rocket,

“Let it off.”
