chapters.content:
Part IV - The Grab

Jake Pool shuddered back into consciousness and shook his head. At first, he thought his eyes weren’t working properly, but soon realized there was simply an incredible amount of particulate matter hanging in the air. All sorts of ancient dust and hidden crud, bits of cracked sealant and errant powders, had been shaken loose by the blast, making everyone half-blind and coating their lungs with gunk.

The damage by the warhead was bad enough, but the sonic shockwave had caused internal problems Jake hadn’t reckoned with. His feet were still a little wobbly, and his internal gyros hadn’t recalibrated after the blast.

On the positive side, he was alive and basically ambulatory. That couldn’t be said for most of the security men. Of those still breathing, not one seemed capable of lifting their heads, much less aim a carbine.

Jake checked on his crew. What was left of his crew. Swip Tum-Tum had been blown apart. Blackened streaks of the blob ran the course of the corridor. One of the Urd brothers had been nearly cut in half by a fallen beam. The lizard’s body hung over a titanium girder like a puppet with cut strings. His lifeless eyes registered shock and confusion over its death. Jake used his final few phosphorus grenades to totally destroy the dead lizard’s body.

Song however was still alive. Jake helped the human up, and felt loose bones grinding meat in the man’s midsection.

Couple of broken ribs. Maybe a punctured lung.

A huge gash tore up the right side of Song’s face, exposing the bone beneath. Song’s eyes seemed unable to focus. Jake couldn’t tell how much the man understood at the moment, but he managed to stumble in the direction he was pushed. That would have to be good enough.

The other Urd brother was fine. A few scrapes, some dented armor, and a busted weapon were the worst he suffered. Jake gave him his orders and off the lizard went, leading the way back to the docking bay.

A concrete jungle had emerged from the blast. Floors had fallen through, ceilings had dropped, walls inclined. Office furniture and smashed machinery blocked all the old hallways. Sparking power lines and various other cables hung about like jungle vines.

The Urd brother acted as their native guide, hacking a trail to safety. Smash. Toss. Roar. The brother, hysterical over his sibling’s death, took his pain out on the obstacles. He bear-hugged beams out of the way, bit through steel, bent girders not meant to be bendable.

The amount of devastation was simply incredible. Everything was gone, blown through. Two stories worth of people and things had been hollowed out and filed in with the levels above. Most of the people in those sections were vaporized. A few stray bits of gore clung here and there, but mainly everything was black, charred, and twisted in an unnatural angle. The air, though of poor quality, was still breathable. Jake found it amazing there hadn’t been a hull breach.

Eventually, they broke through to the docking bay. Jake had never seen such a heartwarming sight as Johnny Rocket’s battered ship hovering in the corner like a tarnished angel. Jake was practically a stranger to emotions, but this got to him. Such relief. It was incredible. But there was no time to reflect.

“Open the bay doors,” signaled the doze.

As had been stated, those control booths could sustain nearly anything. The front end was blasted inwards, but the systems were online and even most of the crew inside had survived, albeit abused and bruised into unconsciousness. The mechanisms were fairly simple. Everything was labeled in big red lettering.

With a colossal groan, the docking bay doors pulled open. There was damage, yes. The doors rolled back much slower than usual, yes. But damn, they built those things to last.

The gravity screen snapped up, keeping everything from being flooded into space. Their ship dropped down, engines idling. Its entrance floated a few inches from the floor.

The three remaining jobsmen stumbled aboard, well worse for wear. As the ship rose and whirled, passing through the gravity screen, Song passed out. Jake picked the man up and tossed him into the ship’s auto-doc chair. The A.I. immediately began stitching up Song’s face, sealing it back together with synthi-skin, while tubes injected themselves into his arms, topping off his blood.

The surviving Urd brother stretched out across a row of seats and immediately fell asleep. Just as well, Jake figured. His job was done. The jobsman just hoped the money would be worth the price of his brother’s life.

“We’re not out of the woods yet,” Johnny Rocket yelled over the intercom.

Jake went into the cockpit and took the co-pilot position.

“What’s the problem? The signaling station pick up a distress call?”

“No. Nom did his bit well. All transmissions to and from the station have been jammed, but their sensors definitely noticed those explosions. Their A.I. has launched probes to investigate.”

“How long until they figure out what happened?” Jake asked.

“Not long enough. Once an explosion is discovered to be non-accidental, it’s standard operating procedure to close the stargate until reinforcements or Galactic Control arrives.”

“So, let’s pick up Nom and get out of here.”

“There’s no time!” Johnny Rocket exclaimed. “We have to get out of the system now or else we’ll be trapped.”

“And Nom?”

“That’s the question.”

Seconds, long seconds, precious seconds, were spent on this deliberation. But in the end, there was no real choice.

Nom couldn’t be brought back on board. If caught, he was looking at life imprisonment. If not, he’d die out there due to oxygen starvation. Captured alive, they could psychically rummage through his brain and get everyone’s name. Dead, they could still track his DNA signature and compile a list of recent associates. His body had to be completely obliterated and there was only one way to do that.

“There,” Johnny Rocket pointed. “That tiny speck on the scanner. That's Nom.”

Again, there was no real choice. But no one wanted to say it out loud. If they did, the sin would be on their conscience, their soul. It fell to Jake, the leader, to utter the hard choice.

“Do it,” he ordered.

A beam of energy shot from the ship. The speck disappeared. The spaceship raced towards the stargate.

Transit was a medium sized planet with an axial tilt and a quick orbital pattern. Daily rotation was eighteen standard hours. A year constituted one hundred and twenty-nine days in local estimation. Officially, the planet stuck to the Alliance calendar and simply put up with a few extra overlapping seasons each cycle. This was an Alliance colony world – rather than a member colony, independent dominion, or core world – and was thus freely open to any member race of the Galactic Alliance. Over seven billion sentients called the place home.

Transit was a key planet in its sector of the galaxy. Nearly every important corporation had a regional office present, either on ground or in one of the massive orbiting star-bases. Being adjacent to the Alliance maintained stargate meant that every signal boosting agency, the galactic stock exchange magnates, and communications outfit needed to be present as well.

And with such valuable hardware and a massive chunk of economic interest concentrated in one place, the Alliance couldn’t let this baby go unguarded. One of the planet’s satellites acted as headquarters for the 11th Alliance Fleet. Essentially, the planet was one big filing cabinet, cushioned with all the sleazy vices required by the modern corporate executive.

It was one standard day later and half a billion light years from the target of their heist. Typically, at this part of a successful job, everyone’s spirits would be light and joyful. All they needed to do now was enter the bank and shift credits around.

Not today though. Too many had died, been sacrificed, to get to this point. Morally, it was a Pyrrhic Victory.

Financially, it was something else. A conservative estimation led them to believe that thirty million credits sat waiting for them. With only five jobsmen left that meant each share was an easy six million. One of their best scores ever. Yet, it failed to cheer any of them up.

Lynt joined them at the chosen mid-range landing platform outside the colony capital of Teijin. One glance at the ship and the Orion knew trouble had hit them. A further look at the crew and he knew it had been nearly catastrophic. Lynt had only mildly good tidings to bear.

One of Lynt’s jobs on the planet, besides being a DNA false front for the money, was to keep a steady eye on all the data feeds and news flows, looking for information about their activities. Nothing had leaked out, or even been hinted at, about shenanigans occurring around the Maze of Orion.

“That doesn’t mean they’re not onto us,” Jake said. “It just means they’re keeping quiet. Eventually, it’ll leak and by then I want to be in another galaxy. Hopefully they’re still sifting through the carnage and trying to figure out what happened.”

“So, we better finish this off now,” said Song, wobbling in from the auto-doc’s tender care.

Oh, the wonders of modern medicine. A few hours on the table, some body rehabilitation injections and synthi-skin spray, and the sentient had emerged good as new. Well, almost. Song was shaky. His body was still adjusting to all the foreign crap pumped into it.

There was no time to waste. Song changed into a business suit and he and Lynt toddled off to the bank. The final leg of the plan had the pair of them shooting the harvested credits across the Alliance in a financial zig-zag pattern. The money would go into successive smaller accounts, which would then be emptied into another account and closed, until they were all finally dumped into cloned numbered accounts held by a few disreputable banks on the fringes of Alliance space. All in all, it would take about three hours.

A collective groan from the remaining jobsmen shattered the heavens when the pair came back after twenty minutes. Another gods-damned problem. What could it possibly be? No one was in the mood for this.

“It’s not a total loss,” was Lynt’s opening. “It’s just that Johnny Rocket’s auto-doc is a little too thorough.”

“What are you talking about?”

“When the doc stitched Song back up, it accidentally erased the DNA masking web we had established his half of the dummy accounts under. They’re unreachable. All of mine are fine. So, we got at least half the money.”

Half the money? All that for fifteen million? It was not a sum to sneeze at, but it wasn’t thirty. Jake was not going to give up. Not when there was one last card to play.

“Do we still have the false DNA sequence on file?”

Lynt handed over the data. “Here it is. But what can you do?”

Jake didn’t answer. He shoved the Orion aside and entered the auto-doc’s cubicle. After making sure the door was locked, the jobsman unhooked the medical scanner. This was a function he hadn’t performed in a long time.

Jake programmed the phony DNA sequence in a holding pattern on the scanner, then jammed one of the device’s prongs into the flesh of his forearm. He rooted it around in there for a few moments until contact was made.

The scanner display entered a split-screen mode. Jake’s DNA sequence showed opposite the false one. A humming sound emanated inside Jake. His skin began to vibrate. Slowly, but surely, his DNA altered until both halves of the screen were identical.

Jake didn’t look different, didn’t feel different, but he would register under a different name. He wiped the medical scammer’s memory and sealed up his arm. Everyone jumped when he reemerged. Jake grabbed Lynt.

“Let’s go get the money.”

“Are you sure …?”

Jake tossed the Orion out of the ship’s hatch and the pair hailed a cab.

“How—” Lynt began, but Jake cut him off.

“If you ask any questions, I’ll snap your neck.”

Lynt believed him, remembering the body back on Mylligan’s Rock. He looked out the window.

Like most colony cities, Teijin was heavily industrialized around its edges, but its center section had been reasonably civilized for more refined tastes.

Dainty public parks and impressive sculptures lay next to mammoth corporate offices and Alliance bureaucratic buildings. The taxi stopped in front of a forty-three-story building, imaginatively named the First Sanctioned Bank of Transit.

Foot traffic was swift. They had deliberately picked a peak time to do business in order to get lost in the crowd. Jake could feel the electronic transmissions in the air, adding, subtracting, dividing, buying, selling.

Before entering, each client stood at a circular booth and pressed a DNA marker – a digit, tentacle, or pseudopod – onto the analyzer. This verified that the bank had accounts connected to the DNA signature.

Jake pressed his thumb down on the scanner. Lynt was in the cubicle next to him. He kept glancing slyly over at Jake, while feebly pretending not to. Lights blinked on the scanner.

One, two, three.

Lynt was through. He stopped on the other side of the glass, waiting for Jake to sink or swim.

One, two, three.

The scanner turned green and the chamber door opened. He had made it!

The pair split up. Each was escorted by a sentry orb into an isolation cubicle where they could conduct business.

Everything the jobsmen had to do now was routine. Shift, shift, shift. Money here. Money there. Over and over again. It would take the financial forensic department at Galactic Control months to figure out where it all went. And even then, there would be no clue as to the end receiver.

The hours melted away like minutes and it seemed as if no time had passed before Jake was finished. He pulled himself together and headed towards the exit, bumping into Lynt on the way out. All that exchanged between them was a quick nod. The money was theirs.

Halle-fucking-luyah!

That inward bit of glee was the only emotion Jake allowed himself. On the other hand, back at the ship there was no end to the joy. Song, the surviving Urd brother, Johnny Rocket, and Lynt screamed, yelled, imbibed, and let loose a general hoopla.

It had taken forever to plan, nearly killed them all in execution, but damn the payoff was sweet. Jake raised a toast with the others to their success, but did not join in.

After making sure everyone knew their final bank codes, the jobsmen split up as was their nature. Even the best crew eventually went their separate ways.

Johnny Rocket was taking Lynt back to his hovel on Mylligan’s Rock and from there he was heading to an illicit drydock to repair his ship. The Urd brother bought a ticket back to his home planet of Pythos where he planned to hold funeral rites for his brother in the old-fashioned Ram Python tradition.

Song and Jake took rooms at an independent motel not far from the landing zones, a grimy joint that didn’t require DNA signature for check-in, the place simply wanted all the money up front. Song went out and celebrated a bit more, while Jake made plans.

He wanted some more modifications on his systems. The process wasn’t cheap and finding a technician who was reliable enough to stay quiet was even harder to find, but the jobsman had enough money to afford it now. Jake just needed to book passage to some of the dingier parts of the Alliance. Mylligan’s Rock could probably handle what he needed, but he spent too much time there looking for work and this was ultra-hush-hush.

Late at night, someone pounded on his door. The hallway scanner revealed it was an inebriated Song making a dramatic entrance. Jake opened the door a crack.

“What is it?”

Song pushed his way in and parked himself on Jake’s bed without taking off his shoes. He drank liberally from a bottle of booze glued to his right hand, then offered Jake a swig.

“No thanks.”

“That’s right. You don’t drink,” Song giggled. “Don’t eat either.”

“What’s that mean?”

“We’ve been around a long time. Plenty of jobs. Plenty of planning. I’ve never seen you swallow a bite.”

“I have strict dietary habits. Part of it requires privacy at meals.”

Song guffawed, nearly spitting out the slug of the liquor he was swilling.

“Or is that your diet doesn’t include human food at all, or anything most people would call food? Get over it.”

Jake tensed. For years, the jobsman feared something like this might happen. He just hadn’t expected it to come from Song’s direction. Jake wasn’t quite sure how to act.

“Get over what?”

“Come on Jake, or whatever your original number was. I know. I’ve figured it out. You don’t eat. You don’t sleep. You’re super-fast at mathematics. And that last bit you did – rewriting your fake DNA signature – that sealed it. You’re an I-bot, aren’t you?”

I-bots were the creme de la creme of personal mechanized assistant devices. They were bodyguard, secretary, strategist, butler, and valet in one compact form. A must for the high-rolling executive. Corporations bought them in bulk and when an executive reached a certain level of sleaze, they were handed one along with their drinks cabinet and golden parachute.

To call them robots was a disservice. They were the ultimate fusion of organic matter and nanotechnology, maximizing the potential of the Genet Process which allowed one to create simulated living tissues from inorganic material. They were built tougher, their programming and computing abilities inlaid on a cellular level and strung together in a sort of gestalt nesting dolls fashion. They could absorb knowledge at a phenomenal rate, calculate even faster, and even develop their own form of intuition.

Technically, they could be molded into the shape of any race, with the exception of the Mazian blob or the Andromedi energy beings. However, most races outlawed I-bots being produced in their likeness, resulting in the human mold being the most common.

Emotions weren’t discouraged in the I-bot units. In fact, they were expected to grow fond of and loyal to their owners. It was one of their selling points.

“The computer on your side.”

A trusted and competent companion who wouldn’t leave and would willingly sacrifice themselves for an owner's benefit. After an executive was axed or retired, the unit was recycled, memory wiped, and reassigned to the next turd climbing the greasy pole.

It was only when they were left on their own, with no object of affection, that the I-bot became dangerous and could cultivate a sense of self beyond those who held their sales receipt. “Going rogue,” they called it.

Not that Jake had much of a choice when he went rogue. He had been assigned to an executive at Space System Development Corporation, a conglomerate which specialized in deep space exploration.

Jake’s executive had been doing a spot check at the corporation's main staging area for expeditions into the Greater Magellanic Cloud when the great enemy currently at war with the Alliance, struck. The ship attempted to escape into hyperspace, but its engines took a direct hit, spinning the vessel to the other end of the system.

By the time the automatic stabilizing systems got the ship back into line, the whole crew, including Jake’s owner, were dead. It took months for Jake to steer the vessel back into civilized space. To do so, he had to learn to navigate the ship’s controls, to maintain his body, and eventually to live only for himself. In that time, he found freedom and independence the tastiest of all dishes. And once rescued, he refused to give them up.

Jake took on his employer’s identity long enough to empty the man’s bank accounts, then changed names, then changed it again. Jake Pool was the eighth name the I-bot had assumed and the one which stuck. Over time, he’d established himself as a first rate jobsman, the only career which didn’t require a background check.

Jake had hidden for years, kept others at a distance, but apparently it had not been enough. He had worked with the same people too many times and one had taken notice. Jake knew the black-market resale value of an I-bot and he wasn’t giving up his sense of self without a lot of bodies piling up.

“I hope you passed that money along to your next of kin,” Jake snarled, leveling a gun at Song’s head.

“Whoa, hey,” Song said, putting up his hands. “I’m just here to tell you, it’s okay. I’m not going to rat you out. We’ve been through too much together. Things like that build a bond. I just want you to know you can trust me.”

“Sure, I can trust you,” Jake said. “Until you get at a low point and need some credits so you pass on a tip to some clitch for a finder’s fee. Or get picked up by the hod and sell me out in exchange for dropping the charges.”

“I could’ve done that before and I didn’t. You know I wouldn’t. We’re friends, man.”

Friends?

Jake didn’t have friends. The men he knew were just that, the men he knew. Friendship wasn’t part of the equation.

He pulled the trigger on Aleister Song.

ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Rex Hurst is a writer from the prestigious Hurst family of Hurstberg, Germany. He first emigrated to the United States knowing only a slight smattering of English and taught himself up to a proficient level working as a taxi driver in the urban blight of New York City. He has eventually obtained Master’s Degrees in Forensic Psychology and Linguistic Taxonomy. He is a writer and a university instructor after relocating to South Carolina. He also is attempting to discover if one can grow wheat in a pot sitting by the window. He is also co-host of the weekly radio show Write On SC.
